Morning · 01

🗂️ Start with the plan

Review the day's learning goals, read approved instructions, and ask the mentor what to observe.

Late morning · 02

🔎 Observe carefully

Watch a permitted demonstration, understand the equipment's purpose, and note questions for the supervisor.

Afternoon · 03

📝 Record clearly

Practise organised documentation or review a training example with guidance. Never invent or alter results.

Wrap-up · 04

🌱 Reflect & grow

Summarise what was learned, note what remains unclear, and agree on the next safe learning step.

10 / NIDHU'S INTERVIEW TOOLKIT

From biomedical basics to interview confidence.

A friendly starter guide for a possible Quality / Regulatory Affairs Trainee or medical-device hardware-related interview. These are practice questions, not confirmed questions from any employer.

🎧

Nidhu's practice room

Tap a question to reveal a simple sample answer. She should adapt answers honestly to her own studies, projects and experience.

⚙️ Hardware basics🧪 Testing & safety📋 Quality systems💬 HR questions
01Tell me about yourself.
What to cover: your biomedical education, one relevant project or subject, strengths such as careful observation, and why you want to learn in medical technology.
Sample framework: “I studied Biomedical Engineering and became interested in how medical technology supports clinical teams. I enjoy learning how devices work, following processes carefully, and documenting information accurately. I’m looking for a role where I can build practical knowledge and learn from experienced professionals.” Make it personal and truthful.
02Why are you interested in quality or regulatory affairs?
Explain that medical devices must meet applicable quality, safety and performance requirements. Quality work helps maintain consistent processes and reliable evidence; regulatory work helps ensure requirements and product documentation are addressed.
Sample idea: “I like that this field combines science, patient impact, structured processes and attention to detail. I’m ready to learn the standards and procedures relevant to the team.”
03What medical equipment do you know?
Choose two or three devices you genuinely understand, such as an ECG machine, patient monitor, infusion pump, ultrasound system or X-ray system. Describe the purpose at a high level, the information or output it provides, and why correct use and maintenance matter. Don't claim hands-on experience you haven't had.
04What would you check before observing a device test?
Follow the approved procedure and supervisor's instructions; confirm the correct device and identification; check that the required setup, tools and calibration status are appropriate; understand the acceptance criteria; and make sure authorised personnel perform the task. Record only what was actually observed. Never operate equipment without training or permission.
05What is the difference between QA and QC?
Quality Assurance (QA) focuses on planned processes that help prevent quality problems and ensure requirements are followed. Quality Control (QC) focuses on checks, inspections or tests used to evaluate whether an output meets specified criteria. Their exact scope depends on the organisation.
06What is an SOP, and why follow it?
An SOP is a controlled, approved instruction for performing a task consistently. Following the current approved version supports repeatability, safety, traceability and compliance. If an instruction is unclear or seems wrong, stop and ask the authorised supervisor rather than improvising.
07What would you do if a test result was missing or unexpected?
Do not guess, copy another result or alter a record. Preserve the record, promptly inform the authorised supervisor, and follow the approved procedure for investigation and documentation. Any repeat test or corrective action must be authorised and documented as required.
08What is calibration?
Calibration compares a measuring instrument's readings with a suitable reference under defined conditions to understand measurement error. Equipment status and records matter because unreliable measurements can affect test conclusions. Calibration is not the same as repairing an instrument.
09How would you handle a task you don't know?
Be honest about the gap, review approved training material, ask focused questions, repeat back important instructions if needed, and perform the task only when authorised and competent. A safe learner asks before acting.
10What do you know about ISO 13485?
It is an international quality-management-system standard designed for organisations involved in medical devices and related services. At trainee level, start by understanding its purpose and the importance of controlled processes, documentation, risk-based thinking and continual compliance; don't pretend to be an expert.
11What is risk management in medical devices?
It is a structured way to identify hazards, estimate and evaluate risks, apply appropriate controls, and review whether those controls are effective throughout the relevant lifecycle. The aim is to reduce risks appropriately while considering the device's intended use.
12Why should we select you as a fresher?
“I may be at the beginning of my professional journey, but I bring curiosity, a willingness to learn, respect for procedures and attention to detail. I will ask when I am unsure, accept feedback and work carefully within my training and responsibilities.”
Support this with one real example from a project, lab, coursework or team activity.
🌱 Remember: These are model ideas, not lines to memorise. Interviewers may ask different questions. Her best answer is clear, honest and grounded in what she actually knows. A fresher is allowed to say, “I don't know yet, but I would learn by…”
